claims.text: A thermal barrier interlayer is needed between plasma-facing tungsten and a CuCrZr heat sink because their operating-temperature ranges are mismatched.
A tungsten-based HEA is currently used as the intermediate layer between tungsten and CuCrZr.
The current tungsten-based HEA interlayer has adequate structural stability but limited heat-transfer capability.
W-based HEAs are promising materials for extreme fusion-reactor environments.
Introducing 5–10 wt% copper into the tungsten-based HEA will form a composite microstructure.
Low-level copper doping will create continuous high-conductivity pathways in the HEA.
The copper phase will form a nano- or microscale network within the HEA matrix.
The copper network will remain sufficiently discontinuous to preserve grain structure and mechanical strength.
Copper's high thermal conductivity will enhance electron and phonon heat transport in the HEA and reduce thermal gradients.
At 5–10 wt% copper, the copper will remain dispersed without significant phase segregation.
Low copper doping will preserve the HEA's high strength and resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
The copper-doped interlayer will have 10–20% higher thermal conductivity than the undoped HEA.
The copper-doped interlayer will retain yield strength and ductility comparable to the undoped HEA.
The predicted benefit will hold at approximately 400–600°C under high heat flux, cyclic mechanical loading, thermal shock, and irradiation.
Copper contents significantly above 5–10 wt% may compromise phase stability or structural integrity.
Prolonged high-temperature irradiation may cause copper segregation or diffusion that negates the thermal and mechanical benefits.
Fusion-reactor plasma-facing materials are exposed to high temperatures, high heat fluxes, energetic particles, and neutron irradiation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes enhanced conduction to continuous copper pathways, whereas the structural mediator says the copper network must remain sufficiently discontinuous. The required topology is therefore internally inconsistent.

The hypothesis describes a low volume fraction of copper, but the intervention specifies 5–10 wt%; volume fraction and weight fraction are not interchangeable without density and composition information.
